pages.t: Understanding aircraft drag: components, relationships and implications
pages.on: Title text and lesson overview; aircraft image with streamlines.
pages.en: Welcome to total drag. In this lesson we build a clear picture of what total drag really is, why it changes so much with speed, and how that drives aircraft performance and efficiency. Total drag is the sum of two main components: parasite drag and induced drag. Parasite drag comes from the aircraft simply moving through the air — skin friction along the surface, form or pressure drag from the shape, and interference drag where components meet, such as the wing–fuselage junction. The key trend is that parasite drag increases rapidly with speed, because dynamic pressure rises with the square of airspeed. Induced drag is different: it appears only because the wing is producing lift. Wing-tip vortices create downwash, which tilts the lift vector slightly rearward, and that rearward component is induced drag. Induced drag is greatest at low speed and high lift demand — take-off, climb and slow flight — and it decreases as speed increases. Add the two together and you get the classic U-shaped total drag curve: on the left side induced drag dominates, on the right side parasite drag dominates. The bottom of the U is the speed for minimum total drag, where induced and parasite drag are equal. That speed is closely linked to practical performance, especially best glide after an engine failure, and is a key reference for efficiency. By the end of this section you should be able to explain why drag behaves the way it does, how weight and altitude shift the curve, and how pilots and designers use these relationships to choose efficient speeds and improve performance.

pages.en: Total drag is best understood as the combination of two main components, and each behaves very differently with speed. Parasite drag comes from the aircraft simply moving through the air. It includes skin-friction drag from air rubbing along the surface, form or pressure drag from the aircraft's shape, and interference drag where airflow is disturbed at junctions such as the wing–fuselage or landing-gear attachments. The key point is that parasite drag rises rapidly with airspeed because it is tied to dynamic pressure, so as speed increases it becomes the dominant part of total drag, especially in cruise and high-speed flight. Induced drag is the drag that appears because the wing is producing lift. A lifting wing creates tip vortices and downwash, which tilt the aerodynamic resultant slightly rearward, producing a rearward component we call induced drag. Induced drag is highest when the aircraft needs a lot of lift — typically at low airspeed and high angle of attack, and at high load factor such as in steep turns. As airspeed increases the required lift coefficient decreases, so induced drag drops significantly. Putting these together explains the classic total-drag picture: at low speed induced drag dominates, at high speed parasite drag dominates, and at an intermediate speed total drag is at its minimum because the two components are balanced.

pages.on: Form (pressure) drag (blunt vs streamlined), interference drag (unfaired vs faired junction), skin friction drag (rough vs smooth surface).
pages.en: Parasite drag is the drag you pay simply for moving an aircraft through the air, and it comes in three main forms. Form, or pressure, drag is caused by the pressure difference between the front and rear of a body. If the airflow separates early, it leaves a large low-pressure wake behind the body, increasing drag. That is why aircraft shapes are streamlined: smooth contours help the flow stay attached longer, shrink the wake and reduce pressure drag, especially around the fuselage, engine nacelles and landing-gear fairings. Interference drag happens where airflows from different components meet and become highly disturbed — at the wing–fuselage junction, strut attachments, flap-track fairings and tail intersections. Even if each part is streamlined on its own, the junction can create extra turbulence and local separation. Designers reduce it with fillets, fairings and smooth blending so the flow passes cleanly from one surface to another. Skin-friction drag comes from the air rubbing against the surface as it flows along in the boundary layer. It depends on wetted surface area, surface roughness, and whether the boundary layer is laminar or turbulent. A smooth, clean airframe — free of contamination, dents, rough paint or protruding fasteners — reduces skin friction. That is why maintenance and surface condition matter: small roughness can increase drag and reduce performance, especially in cruise.

pages.t: Parasite drag and speed relationship: the quadratic effect
pages.on: Dp = ½ρV²·S·CD; variables; graph Dp vs V ("drag increase factor of 2" label); implications for design and flight.
pages.en: Parasite drag rises quickly with speed because it is driven by dynamic pressure, which grows with the square of velocity. The standard drag equation is D = ½ρV²·S·CD, where rho is air density, V is airspeed, S is the reference area and CD is the drag coefficient. The key part is V². If you double the airspeed, the dynamic pressure becomes four times larger, so with the same configuration and roughly the same CD, parasite drag increases by about a factor of four. That is why parasite drag dominates at high speed. At low speed induced drag is usually the bigger concern, because the wing must work at a high lift coefficient; but as speed increases, induced drag falls while parasite drag climbs rapidly. In practical terms this relationship limits maximum speed, drives fuel burn in fast cruise, and explains why a small increase in cruise speed can need a disproportionately large increase in power or thrust. For designers, reducing parasite drag means refining shapes, smoothing junctions and improving surface finish. For pilots, it explains why flying faster than an efficient cruise speed costs a lot of fuel: the aircraft is pushing against a drag force that rises steeply with speed.

pages.on: Three panels: wingtip vortices, downwash creation, lift vector tilt (tilted lift vector → induced drag component).
pages.en: Induced drag comes directly from the way a wing produces lift in three-dimensional flow. Wing-tip vortices form because the pressure is higher under the wing and lower above it. Near the tips, high-pressure air from the underside spills around to the top and rolls up into two trailing, counter-rotating vortices. Those vortices create downwash, a downward deflection of the airflow behind the wing. This downwash means the local relative wind at the wing is tilted slightly downward compared with the free stream. Because the wing now sees a tilted airflow, its aerodynamic resultant is not perpendicular to the flight path — the lift force is effectively tilted rearward. When you resolve that tilted force into components, the rearward component is induced drag: the unavoidable drag associated with producing lift.

pages.on: Lift coefficient (CL; doubling CL quadruples induced drag), aspect ratio (glider vs low-AR fighter), wingtip devices (winglets vs none).
pages.en: Induced drag is controlled mainly by how much lift the wing must produce and how efficiently it produces it. One, the lift coefficient CL: induced drag rises very quickly with lift demand because CDi = k·CL². If CL increases, induced drag increases quadratically — that is why it is most noticeable in slow flight, climb and turns, when the wing needs a higher CL. Two, aspect ratio, AR: a higher-aspect-ratio wing generates less downwash for the same lift, so it produces weaker vortices and less induced drag. In coefficient form k = 1 ÷ (π·e·AR), so increasing AR reduces k and therefore reduces induced drag. This is why gliders with long, slender wings are so efficient at low speed. Three, wing-tip devices: winglets, raked tips and other tip treatments reduce the strength of the tip-vortex system by limiting pressure leakage around the tip and reshaping the flow. The result is lower effective induced drag for the same lift, improving range and fuel efficiency — one reason winglets are common on modern airliners. Putting it together: induced drag gets worse when you need more lift, and it gets better when the wing produces that lift with less vortex and downwash loss — mainly through higher aspect ratio and smarter wing-tip flow control.

pages.on: Di ∝ 1/V² (doubling speed reduces induced drag by a factor of four); low-speed implications; high-speed behaviour; total drag components graph (image shrunk on the page).
pages.en: Induced drag falls with speed because the wing needs a smaller lift coefficient to support the aircraft as speed increases. In steady level flight, lift is approximately equal to weight, so CL = 2W ÷ (ρV²S). As V increases, the required CL drops roughly with 1/V². The induced drag coefficient follows CDi = k·CL², so when speed goes up, CL goes down and induced drag drops sharply. In terms of force, induced drag decreases approximately with 1/V² for a given weight and configuration at a given density. Low-speed implications: during take-off, climb, approach and landing you are flying slower and often at a higher angle of attack, which means a higher CL. That makes induced drag a large part of total drag, so you need more power or thrust to overcome it, especially when trying to maintain a climb or arrest a sink rate at low speed. High-speed behaviour: as speed increases, induced drag becomes relatively small while parasite drag rises rapidly with V². This is why in cruise and high-speed flight the aircraft is mostly paying for parasite drag, and why streamlining and surface cleanliness matter so much at higher speeds. So the practical picture is: slow flight is induced-drag dominated, fast flight is parasite-drag dominated, and the shift between the two shapes both aircraft design and how pilots choose efficient speeds.

pages.t: The total drag–speed graph: understanding aerodynamic efficiency
pages.on: Induced drag (Di ∝ 1/V²), parasite drag (Dp ∝ V²), total drag U-curve; "minimum drag speed (best efficiency)"; "cruise flight (operating near minimum drag speed)".
pages.en: The total drag–speed graph combines the two main drag trends into one picture that pilots and engineers use all the time. One, the induced drag curve, dominant on the left side. At low speed the wing must produce lift at a high lift coefficient, which creates strong tip vortices and downwash, so induced drag is high. As speed increases the required lift coefficient drops, so induced drag decreases rapidly. This is why induced drag is most noticeable in take-off, climb, slow flight and steep turns. Two, the parasite drag curve, dominant on the right side. Parasite drag comes from skin friction, form drag and interference drag; it depends on dynamic pressure, so it increases with speed, roughly following V². At higher speeds it becomes the dominant component and a key limit on maximum speed and fuel efficiency. Three, the total drag curve, U-shaped. Total drag is the sum of induced and parasite drag. Because one decreases while the other increases, the total forms a U. The bottom of the U is the speed for minimum total drag, where induced and parasite drag are equal. Why this graph matters operationally: the minimum-drag point corresponds to best glide, maximum L/D. Flying slower than this puts you in the induced-drag-dominated region, with more power required to maintain speed and altitude. Flying faster pushes you into parasite-drag dominance, where power required rises quickly with speed. So the U-curve is the road map for choosing efficient speeds and understanding why performance changes so much between slow flight and high-speed cruise.

pages.t: Speed for minimum drag: achieving maximum aerodynamic efficiency
pages.on: Intersection point (Di = Dp, minimum total drag); best glide speed; operational significance; graph with Vmd.
pages.en: The speed for minimum drag is at the bottom of the total drag curve. It is where induced drag equals parasite drag — the speed at which the decreasing induced-drag curve and the increasing parasite-drag curve contribute equally. At that point total drag is as small as it can be for that configuration and weight, so the aircraft needs the least thrust to keep flying steadily. This speed is the best-glide speed. In an engine-out glide the goal is to maximise the glide ratio — distance travelled per height lost — which corresponds to maximum L/D, and maximum L/D occurs at the minimum-total-drag speed. So flying at this speed gives the greatest glide distance in still air. Operationally it is a useful performance anchor point. Pilots do not normally fly at the minimum-drag speed: cruise is usually faster for time and efficiency trade-offs, and approaches are slower for control and landing distance. But knowing this point helps you understand why power required rises when you fly too slow (induced drag dominated) or too fast (parasite drag dominated), and it is especially important for engine-out planning, glide performance and energy management.

pages.t: Effect of aircraft mass on drag
pages.on: Total drag vs airspeed for lighter and heavier aircraft (curve higher and to the right); Vmd (lighter) < Vmd (heavier); increased induced drag; speed for minimum drag increases.
pages.en: As aircraft mass increases, the aeroplane must generate more lift to maintain level flight, because lift has to match weight. The easiest way to see the drag effect is through the lift coefficient: at any given speed a heavier aircraft needs a higher CL to produce the extra lift. Since induced drag follows CDi = k·CL², that higher CL drives induced drag up significantly, especially on the low-speed side of the drag curve. On a total drag–speed graph this raises the left side of the U — the induced-drag-dominated region — and moves the minimum point to a higher speed, with a higher minimum drag. The speed for minimum drag therefore increases with mass: a heavier aircraft must fly faster to reach the same efficient CL where induced and parasite drag balance. In practice this means best-glide speed and other efficiency reference speeds increase with weight. A useful rule of thumb is that these optimum speeds scale with the square root of weight, V_opt ∝ √W. If weight increases, the most efficient speed increases; if weight decreases, it decreases. Operationally this matters for flight planning and fuel efficiency: flying too slowly when heavy pushes the aircraft deep into the induced-drag region and increases power required, while flying at the appropriate higher speed keeps it near the minimum-drag condition and improves efficiency for that weight.

pages.on: 1 drag vs IAS: "drag curve shifts downward due to lower air density… less drag for a given IAS at higher altitudes"; 2 drag vs TAS: minimum drag occurs at higher TAS at high altitude, "similar drag values for a given TAS across altitudes"; 3 operational implications.
pages.en: Pressure altitude changes drag mainly through air density, and the key is whether you plot drag against IAS or TAS. One, drag versus IAS: IAS is essentially a measure of dynamic pressure. At higher altitude the air is less dense, but for a given IAS the dynamic pressure is the same, so the aircraft feels the same aerodynamic loading, needs the same CL and has the same drag. Plotted against IAS (strictly EAS), the drag curve therefore stays in the same place at every altitude, as long as compressibility can be ignored. Two, drag versus TAS: to hold the same IAS at higher altitude you must fly a higher TAS — more true speed through thinner air to create the same dynamic pressure. Plotted against TAS, the whole curve moves to the right with altitude: the minimum drag is the same value but it occurs at a higher TAS. At very high altitude and higher Mach numbers, compressibility can increase CD and change the picture. Three, operational implications: this is why aircraft can cruise efficiently at altitude — for the same drag you travel at a higher true airspeed, which improves range for certain operating points. But you must consider the higher TAS and the power it needs (power = drag × TAS), engine and propeller efficiency, temperature and Mach limits. In flight planning, altitude selection is a trade between aerodynamic efficiency, engine performance, winds and time, which is why the optimum cruise altitude changes as weight decreases during the flight.

pages.on: Graph of total drag vs airspeed: "stable region" panel over the descending (left) branch and "unstable region" over the rising (right) branch; examples high-speed cruise (self-correcting) and low-speed approach (requires intervention).
pages.en: Speed stability comes from the slope of the thrust- or power-required curve, which mirrors the total drag curve. The key question is: if speed changes a little, does the aeroplane tend to return to the trimmed speed or drift away? The stable region has a positive slope — the right side of the curve, the higher-speed side. There, total drag increases as speed increases. If the aircraft momentarily speeds up, drag rises, so with the same thrust it loses the extra speed and settles back. If it slows slightly, drag reduces, so the same thrust is now more than enough and it accelerates back toward the trimmed speed. Small speed disturbances tend to self-correct. The unstable region has a negative slope — the left side of the curve, the lower-speed side, often called the region of reverse command. There the relationship flips: slowing down requires more thrust or power to hold altitude, because induced drag grows rapidly. If the aircraft slows a little while thrust stays the same, it may not have enough excess thrust to recover, and the speed can keep decreasing unless the pilot adds power and/or reduces the angle of attack. Likewise, if it speeds up slightly, drag may reduce and let it accelerate further. In this region holding a steady speed requires active control. The practical takeaway: on the right side speed control feels easy and naturally stable; on the left side it is touchy, and you often manage speed with power and the flight path with pitch, especially in slow flight and on approach.

pages.on: Four-step chain: speed reduction → drag increase → further deceleration → stall risk; example: approach and landing.
pages.en: In the unstable region on the left side of the drag or power curve — the region of reverse command — a small speed disturbance can grow into a bigger problem if you do not correct it. Speed reduction is the trigger: the aircraft slows slightly, perhaps from a gust, increased bank, a small pitch change, or simply being a little slow on approach. To hold altitude at the new lower speed, the wing needs a higher lift coefficient, which means a higher angle of attack. That higher lift demand brings a drag increase: induced drag rises rapidly at low speed, so in this region slowing down increases drag rather than reducing it. If power is not increased, the aircraft no longer has enough excess thrust to overcome the higher drag, and you get further deceleration. The extra drag bleeds off more speed, which forces an even higher angle of attack to hold lift, which increases induced drag again. That is the feedback loop: slower leads to more drag, which leads to even slower. If the cycle continues, the stall risk increases, because the angle of attack is being pushed toward the critical value. The key safety point is that this is not fixed by pulling to hold the nose up. Pulling increases the angle of attack and can accelerate the problem. The correct response is to add power and reduce any excessive angle of attack — lower the nose as needed to recover speed — then re-establish the desired flight path once energy is restored.

pages.on: Polar diagram: high aspect ratio (glider, less induced drag) vs low aspect ratio (fighter, more induced drag); formula CD = CD0 + k·CL², k = 1/(π·e·AR).
pages.en: The CL–CD relationship, the drag polar, is a powerful way to see how efficiently a wing produces lift, because it shows the drag cost of a given CL. A useful simplification is CD ≈ CD0 + k·CL², where k = 1 ÷ (π·e·AR). So the big driver of wing-to-wing differences is the k term, which depends strongly on aspect ratio. High-aspect-ratio wings, like gliders, have a smaller k: the polar is tighter and does not move to the right as quickly as CL increases. In practice, as the glider asks for more lift — higher CL at low speed — the induced drag penalty grows more slowly. That keeps L/D higher, improves climb and soaring efficiency, and gives excellent glide performance, especially in the low-to-moderate speed range where induced drag matters most. Low-aspect-ratio wings, common on many fighter designs, have a larger k, so induced drag rises faster with CL. On the polar the curve swings right more aggressively as lift increases — more drag for the same CL, particularly at high lift demand, tight turns and slow flight. The trade is that low-AR wings can be structurally strong, support high-g manoeuvring and suit sweep and transonic design priorities. Fighters also rely on high thrust and often use leading-edge extensions, vortex lift and high-lift controls to get the required lift and handling despite the induced drag cost. So the takeaway is: higher aspect ratio improves the CL–CD curve by reducing induced drag, while lower aspect ratio sacrifices low-speed efficiency to gain other advantages important for high-speed and manoeuvring flight.
pages.th: ความสัมพันธ์ CL–CD หรือ drag polar เป็นวิธีที่ทรงพลังในการดูว่าปีกสร้างแรงยกได้อย่างมีประสิทธิภาพแค่ไหน เพราะแสดงต้นทุนแรงต้านของ CL หนึ่ง ๆ การประมาณที่มีประโยชน์คือ CD ≈ CD0 + k·CL² โดย k = 1 ÷ (π·e·AR) ตัวขับหลักของความต่างระหว่างปีกแต่ละแบบจึงเป็นเทอม k ซึ่งขึ้นกับ aspect ratio อย่างมาก ปีก aspect ratio สูงอย่างเครื่องร่อนมี k เล็ก polar จึงแคบและไม่เบนไปทางขวาเร็วเมื่อ CL เพิ่ม ในทางปฏิบัติ เมื่อเครื่องร่อนต้องการแรงยกมากขึ้น คือ CL สูงขึ้นที่ความเร็วต่ำ ค่าปรับจากแรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำจะเพิ่มช้ากว่า ทำให้ L/D สูงอยู่ ไต่และ soaring ได้มีประสิทธิภาพ และร่อนได้ดีเยี่ยม โดยเฉพาะในช่วงความเร็วต่ำถึงปานกลางที่แรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำมีผลมากที่สุด ปีก aspect ratio ต่ำ ซึ่งพบในเครื่องขับไล่หลายแบบ มี k ใหญ่ แรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำจึงเพิ่มเร็วตาม CL บน polar เส้นโค้งเบนไปทางขวาแรงกว่าเมื่อแรงยกเพิ่ม คือแรงต้านมากกว่าที่ CL เดียวกัน โดยเฉพาะเมื่อต้องการแรงยกสูง เลี้ยวแคบ และบินช้า ข้อแลกเปลี่ยนคือปีก AR ต่ำมีโครงสร้างแข็งแรง รองรับการบินที่ g สูง และเข้ากับการออกแบบปีกลู่และ transonic เครื่องขับไล่ยังพึ่งแรงขับสูง และมักใช้ leading-edge extension, vortex lift และระบบควบคุมแรงยกสูง เพื่อให้ได้แรงยกและการบังคับที่ต้องการแม้จะต้องจ่ายแรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำ สรุปคือ aspect ratio ที่สูงขึ้นปรับปรุงกราฟ CL–CD โดยลดแรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำ ส่วน aspect ratio ต่ำยอมเสียประสิทธิภาพที่ความเร็วต่ำเพื่อแลกข้อได้เปรียบอื่นที่สำคัญต่อการบินความเร็วสูงและการต่อสู้

pages.on: Text: 1 total drag composition; 2 speed and altitude effects; 3 design implications; 4 operational considerations.
pages.en: Total drag is best remembered as the sum of parasite drag and induced drag. Parasite drag comes from skin friction, form and interference effects and increases rapidly with speed, while induced drag is created by lift production — vortices and downwash — and is most significant at low speed and high lift demand. Their opposite trends produce the familiar U-shaped total drag curve, which explains why power required rises when you fly too slow or too fast. Speed and altitude influence these components in different ways. Increasing speed shifts you toward parasite-drag dominance, while slowing down increases induced drag because the wing must operate at a higher lift coefficient. With altitude, density decreases, which changes the relationship between IAS and TAS: at the same IAS the drag is the same but the TAS is higher, and compressibility becomes relevant at higher Mach numbers. From a design perspective, managing drag means shaping the aircraft to reduce parasite drag and designing the wing to reduce induced drag. Higher aspect ratio, a good spanwise lift distribution and devices like winglets lower induced drag, while streamlined shapes, clean junctions and smooth surfaces reduce parasite drag. Weight is also critical: heavier aircraft need more lift, which increases induced drag and shifts the optimum speeds upward. Operationally, these principles lead to better decisions. Pilots and planners use them to select efficient cruise speeds and altitudes, anticipate performance changes with weight and configuration, and manage energy safely, especially in slow flight, where induced drag and speed-stability issues become important. Understanding the drag picture helps optimise fuel burn, range and margins while keeping the aircraft in the right part of its performance envelope.

numbers: Total drag = parasite + induced; Dp ∝ V², Di ∝ W²/V² (level flight, same density).
Double the speed → parasite drag × 4 (parasite power × 8), induced drag ÷ 4.
VMD: Di = Dp, minimum total drag, maximum L/D = best glide (still air). C172S best glide 68 KIAS at 2,550 lb (POH — confirm, SME).
VMD ∝ √W; minimum drag ∝ W; max L/D (glide ratio) unchanged by weight.
Drag vs IAS/EAS: same curve at every altitude (no compressibility). Drag vs TAS: curve moves right, same minimum drag. Power required = D × TAS → increases with altitude.
Speed stable above VMD (positive slope); back side / region of reverse command below VMD (for propeller aircraft, practically below VMP).
CD = CD0 + CL² ÷ (π·e·AR); AR (type data — SME): C172S ≈ 7.4, DA42 ≈ 11.
corr: Drag vs IAS "shifts downward… less drag for a given IAS at higher altitude"; "similar drag values for a given TAS across altitudes".
Same IAS/EAS → same drag at any altitude; vs TAS the curve moves right with the same minimum drag. Power required rises with altitude.
"Stable region" drawn over the negative-slope branch, "unstable region" over the positive-slope branch.
Reversed: stable = right/positive slope (above VMD), unstable = left/negative slope (below VMD).
VMD labelled "best glide/cruise"; "cruise flight (operating near minimum drag speed)".
VMD = best glide; piston aircraft cruise well above VMD.
Infographic shrunk in the middle of the page.
Speed-stability boundary given as the drag curve only.
For propeller aircraft the practical boundary is VMP on the power-required curve (below VMD) — note for instructors.
